It is a general belief that Christians who attend church regularly are more holy than those that don’t.

Herbo knows that he has done things that are condemned by Christianity—murder and theft—so he doesn’t go to Church to avoid posturing himself as holy. Regardless of his sins he believes God is with him—a reference to the idea of God’s forgiveness.

While changing the color of someone’s shirt might initially sound like a magic trick like Herb suggests, the fact that he specifically recalls making the color burgundy (a deep reddish brown) out of fifty white t-shirts is an allusion to blood staining the clothing of homicide victims.

G Herbo is from the Southside of Chicago, and although crime rates have been falling in the city, 573 people were killed in the city in 2024, with Chicago having the highest homicide rate for the past seven years in U.S. cities home to over a million people. Herbo recalls the violence-ridden environment he grew up in, not too dissimilar to his past collaborator and fellow Chicago native Polo G, who rapped a similar line to this one on his 2021 hit track, “RAPSTAR”:

Homicides when we lurk, I'ma step ‘til my feet hurt

White tees turned burgundy t-shirts

line: Shoutout my nigga Gotti, man, on bro

Herb shouts out Memphis, Tennesee rapper Yo Gotti whose 2006 track “That’s What’s Up (Intro)” is the instrumental that he raps over on this track. In 2012, Gotti founded the record label CMG (Collective Music Group) which Herb reps on the verse’s opening line.

Herb—referring to either his own tendency to rep CMG or Gotti's—compares it to repping EBK, an acronym for “Everybody Killa.” Herb is saying he will get violent or active with anybody regardless of their affiliation. Given how Herb shouts out Gotti and is rapping on his beat, it might be fair to say that he’s repping CMG (and in turn, EBK) a great deal.

line: I told Glo she good in the ’Raq, I was drunk in Memphis like Mac Snoop (Yeah)
vault_lines: I told Glo she good in the 'Raq, I was drunk in Memphis like Mac Snoop (Yeah)
meaning:
“Glo” is a nickname for Memphis, Tennessee rapper GloRilla, known for her hit tracks like 2022’s “F.N.F. (Let’s Go),” and 2024’s “Yeah Glo!” and “TGIF.” GloRilla and G Herbo actually collaborated together alongside Mello Buckzz for Herbo’s 2023 tape Strictly 4 My Fans 2 on the song, “Outside.”

Herb says Glo is welcome in “the ‘Raq,” a nickname meaning “Chiraq,” comparing the war-torn streets of his home city of Chicago, Illinois to the history of armed conflicts in the country of Iraq. In turn, Herbo recounts going to Glo’s home city and getting as drunk as Mac Snoop, a local Memphis artist and social media personality whose social media content seems to be as much about drinking as it is about his desire to quit. In a vlog from November 2025 featuring Mac Snoop, he is offered $10,000 to stop drinking and that same month, Mac released a song, titled “Ooh Wee I’m Bout To Stop Drinking.”

It’s also worth noting that this allusion to GloRilla is purposeful because she is a Memphis artist who signed to Yo Gotti’s CMG record label. Gotti’s 2006 track “That’s What’s Up (Intro)” is the instrumental Herbo remixes on this song, giving Gotti a shoutout in the track’s intro.

line: Drac’ go hackin’ ’em like Shaq (Grra), we whacked him ’cause he lacked (Whacked)
vault_lines: Drac' go hackin' 'em like Shaq (Grra), we whacked him 'cause he lacked (Whacked)
meaning:
G Herbo employs wordplay to reference basketball defensive strategy “Hack-a-Shaq.” The move is used in the NBA—acronym for National Basketball Association—which involves committing intentional fouls for the purpose of lowering opponents scoring. The word was notably named after former basketball player Shaquille O'Neal, making the meaning of the name clear.



GIF: Hack-A-Shaq strategy used in the basketball court.

A “Drac'” or a “Draco” is slang for an automatic firearm. Nonetheless, for a Draco to “hack ‘em like Shaq” implies the gun being fired at a rival member, primarily affirming the deadly effect on an individual—since the basketball technique is used to slow a player down on the court, thus, asserting the play of words.

Hailing from Chicago himself, “Raq'” is an abbreviation for “Chiraq,” which is a combination of the two words “Chicago” and “Iraq.” The word depicts the similarities between Iraq’s wars due to the proximate murder rates.

A “Caddy” refers to a Cadillac Escalade, a model typically used for seclusion, hence its blacked-out window tinting. Ultimately, a “bulletproof Caddy” notably displays G Herbo’s gang ties—also affirms his self-protection due to his popularity.

line: Vito, Kobe, Cap, and Roc
meaning:
Here, Herb shouts out multiple close friends that he has lost, names that should be familiar to fans of Herb’s music.

First, Herb shouts out Vito, a member of No Limit who sadly passed away in 2009. Not much is known about Vito due to him passing away five years before the launch of Herbs rap career with the release of the Pistol P Project, but he was evidently a beloved member of the gang; No Limit members set April 27th, the day Vito tragically lost his life, as “Vito Day” in order to commemorate him.



Next, Herb shouts out Kobe, another close friend of Herb and longtime member of No Limit who tragically lost his life in 2013. Kobe has been mentioned numerous times throughout Herb’s discography, most notably with Herb’s 2016 album “Ballin Like I’m Kobe,” named after his fallen friend and showcasing his headstone on the cover.

A throwback photo of G Herbo (left) and Kobe (right).



Then, Herb shouts out fellow rapper GBE Capo, who tragically passed away in 2015. Capo was part of Chief Keef’s Glory Boyz label but also was a member of No Limit. Capo and Herb have also collaborated musically over the years, with releases such as Forced to Shooting, Bein Famous, Fake Niggas, and more.



Finally, Herb shouts out a highly influential member of No Limit, Lil Roc, who sadly passed away in 2012. Roc was a very beloved member of No Limit, and after his passing No Limit members would start claiming “Roc Block” in memory of their fallen friend, with Herb even utilizing it in his music.

line: Yeah, yeah, I turned a serial killer to a rapper
vault_lines: Yeah, yeah, I turned a serial killer to a rapper
meaning:
Lil Durk is referring to his late friend, fellow Chicago native and former labelmate King Von. The line between artistry and real life is often blurred when it comes to the violent subject matter illustrated in drill music. However, in King Von’s case, numerous bars and phrases within his discography could seemingly be linked to real life crimes. Von had been implicated in murder cases before, and his history with violent crimes was heavily debated in subreddits like r/Chiraqology.

This particular topic was eventually covered by hip-hop journalist Trap Lore Ross in his April 2023 YouTube video titled, “King Von: Rap’s First Serial Killer.” This video is undoubtedly what Durk is referencing with this bar, as the documentary was incredibly pressing due to the fact that Ross argued that Von fit the FBI’s definition of a serial killer. The video contained extensive research into King Von’s life before his untimely passing in November 2020, with Ross cross-referencing the Chicago rapper’s lyrics with actual real-life murders that took place in Chicago.



The thumbnail for Ross' King Von documentary

Durk makes it clear with this line that he isn’t interested in this narrative, a sentiment he reiterated when he vaguely acknowledged the video’s existence in an April 2023 interview with XXL, advising his listeners to focus on the times which he broadcasted Von’s upstanding character. Again on, “In The Air,” it appears as if Durk is uninterested in an entertaining a narrative that he transformed Von from a shooter into a rap supertstar.

Herb shouts out the block he was raised on, 79th Street and Essex Avenue on the South Side of Chicago, Illinois. 79th and Essex, Roc block

We from 79th and Essex, “Roc Block,” named after my brother Roc (RIP). That’s where we all grew up. The way I rap. The way I do everything. Everything about me.

line: Glock 23 got a switch on a back (Rrr)
vault_lines: Glock 23 got a switch on a back (Rrr)
meaning:
As many avid rap fans already know, a “switch” is a device that can be attached to various types of guns—although most commonly with Glock-branded handguns—that operates as a form of auto sear, allowing the firearm to fire fully automatic when it normally couldn’t. It does this through holding the trigger bar down to stop it from limiting fire to one round per trigger pull.

When attached, a switch allows for both semi- and fully-automatic fire settings through a button; to the left the handgun stays in semi-automatic, but by pushing the button to the right, the trigger bar is held down and rounds are continuously fed until there’s no more ammo left.

Because of this, a switch by itself is considered a machine gun by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives (ATF) without even needing to be attached to a firearm.

G Herbo announces that he doesn’t have to return to Atlanta, Georgia because he has had sex with all of the city’s women—not unlike a claim he makes about his home city of Chicago in the same bar.

“The ‘Raq” is short for “Chiraq,” a slang term that refers to Chicago, combining the first half of its name with the of country of Iraq’s to compare the city’s gang wars to the actual militant conflicts in the Middle East. Both “the 'Raq” and “Chiraq” are terms heard all throughout Herbo’s music and Chicago drill as a whole. Herbo has previously claimed to have had sex with all of the 'Raq’s women on his September 2022 track, “Blues,” featuring Atlanta rapper, Future:

I’m a renegade, ain’t no checkin' me, and everybody in the ‘Raq know (Know that)
I been fucked all the 'Raq hoes (Phew)

He also mentions how he flew to Atlanta with frequent collaborator and good friend Sizzle, more widely known as Southside, the producer of this very song amongst countless others in G Herbo’s discography. Southside’s home city of Atlanta is home to several prominent hip-hop figureheads, a point Herbo enunciates on the Big Swerv track, “In The A” where he firstly name-dropped Southside alongside other Atlanta artists like 21 Savage and Young Thug (also known as Slatt, Spider or King Slime):

I’m in the A, havin' my way like Slime and ‘em (Free Spider)
21, his truck in front, I’m right behind him (Right behind him)
I’m in the A, havin’ my way like Sizzle and ‘em

This is significant because both Sizzle and Slatt (Young Thug) are referenced again in this bar for a second allusion to the city of Atlanta. Aside from being a good friend of the two Atlanta artists he named, Herbo’s name-drops also serve as a call to action for the government to free Young Thug, as at the time of Big Swerv’s release, the rapper was on trial and charged with conspiracy to violate the RICO act, something he had been arrested and fighting legally ever since May 9, 2022.

line: Humble beast, that’s still me, but I’m the chosen one at that
vault_lines: Humble beast, that's still me, but I'm the chosen one at that
meaning:
Reiterating how he remained a humble beast seven years later, Herbo calls back to the title of his 2017 debut album, Humble Beast. In October 2017, the Chicago rapper spoke with Billboard about what his then upcoming album’s title meant:

Being in the streets, you gotta be humble. You gotta approach every situation humbly because you never know what you’re gonna have to do to get out of that situation. It’s possessing that humble trait, and still being a beast to get yourself out of any situation by any means, being fearless—that’s me. Growing up in the streets—the “jungle”—you’re gonna turn into a beast. It’s gonna turn you into an animal. But you gotta approach a situation humbly, because you never know when you’re going to have to use that trait.

It’s clear that upon the release of Big Swerv, Herb feels conflicted, viewing himself as someone who has to remain humble after surviving his rough upbringing in the Chicago streets, yet he feels “chosen,” having now acquired more fame and amenities that came with a successful rap career.

Tom Brady was a quarterback who played in the National Football League for 23 total seasons with the New England Patriots and later the Tampa Bay Bucaneers. He is widely considered one of the greatest football players of all time.

When Herbo says people remind of him Tom Brady, and how they never wanted a sack, he is using “sack” as a homonym for both a sack of money, as well as getting “sacked” in the sport of football. A sack is what happens when a member of the defending team manages to tackle the quarterback while they are in possession of the ball, and Tom Brady being his team’s quarterback wouldn’t want that to happen, as it would set his team back.



Tom Brady getting sacked

This is all an ellaborate way for Herbo to allege that his opposition really isn’t committed to acquiring money, or a “sack” in the same way Tom Brady wouldn’t want to get sacked on the field.

With plaques and plaques, and plaques
meaning:
Herbo is using “plaque” as a homonym for both the plaques awarded by the RIAA as well as the bacteria that lines teeth and causes decay and disease.

Custom plaques are awarded to musicians by the Recording Industry Association of America whenever their sound recordings sell a certain amount of units. These certifications range from gold, platinum, multi-platinum, and diamond. Herbo raps that he won’t be able to sleep until his house is lined with these plaques (or until he is recognized for the hit tracks he makes). He equates this goal to bacterial plaque rapidly spreading throughout human teeth—spreading disease if not treated properly.

At the time of this song’s release, Herb had a gold album for his February 2020 project, PTSD, as well as a certified platinum single for the title track of the same album. The Chicago rapper had also acquired three additional certifications for his guest appearances on other artists' songs.

meaning:
The term “G-Fazos” refers to a pair of all-white Nike Air Force 1’s. Originally popularized by Herb himself, the nickname was created as a way of memorializing one of his long time friends Fazon Robinson (known as G Fazo), a beloved member of NLMB who was a victim of gun violence and sadly passed away in April of 2010.



Pictured above is G Fazo (NLMB). RIP.




Before he passed, Fazo was always seen wearing a fresh pair of white Nike Air Forces. His love for them was so strong that once one pair got dirty, he’d be buying a brand new pair to wear in their place. The term “G-Fazos” was ultimately popularized in Herb’s 2015 track titled Rollin' through the legendary lyric:

Do your thing, just don’t step on these all white G-Fazo’s, you hear me?



This photo of Fazo's room was allegedly taken the day that he had passed away. As seen in the photo, Fazo owned at least a dozen pairs of Air Force 1's.




The memorializing of Fazo doesn’t just end at the music, as Herb himself has admitted in multiple interviews that he has adopted Fazo’s love for the Air Force 1. In an interview with djvlad from 2016, Herb estimated that he’s “probably spent like two hundred thousand” on Air Force 1’s; being almost nine years ago, it’s very likely this number has only grown exponentially.

line: He was Lakeside, got his ass blazed
vault_lines: He was Lakeside, got his ass blazed
meaning:
In this lyric, Herb sends a diss to what is assumed to be long-time rival KTS Dre and the entirety of Lakeside.



Lakeside is a faction of Gangster Disciples, but No Limit’s real enemies were a smaller set from Lakeside known as KTS, or Kill to Survive. Due to an area of overlap between the territories of these two gangs, disputes were both common and bloody, with many lives being senselessly lost on both sides; most notably, No Limit’s Mad Maxx, who Herb has shouted out countless times, and KTS' Von and Dre.

A map depicting the approximate territories of No Limit and Lakeside.

Although the death of KTS Von is believed to be unrelated to the conflict between No Limit and KTS, many longtime fans of Herb believe that No Limit is somehow associated with the death of KTS Dre. In July of 2021, one day after his bail was posted, Dre was shot approximately 34 times and killed right in front of the Cook County Jail. His grandmother, who was there to pick him up, was also injured but thankfully survived.

line: Wasn’t even worryin’ ’bout 50 Cent Young, hit niggas with them buck, buck, buck, buck, buck, buck (G Herbo, Big Swerve)
vault_lines: Wasn't even worryin' 'bout 50 Cent
Young, hit niggas with them buck, buck, buck, buck, buck, buck (G Herbo, Big Swerve)
meaning:
Herbo refers to the G-Unit rapper 50 Cent and slyly alludes to his former labelmate, Young Buck.

Swervo is basically saying he was not worried about acquiring money or fifty cents (50 Cent) because he was outside shooting and surviving in harsh, violent conditions. Imitating the sound of a firearm, the Chicago rapper asserts how he was young, before repeating the sound, “buck,” demonstrating how he had to fire his gun, while hiding Young Buck’s name within the bar.

Young Buck signed to 50 Cent’s G-Unit label in 2003, and the two released several collaborations, including “Blood Hound” (Feb. 2003) which appeared on 50 Cent’s Get Rich or Die Tryin'. The pair were on good terms for a number of years until numerous issues appeared between the two as business partners. In 2008, Young Buck was expelled from the G-Unit rap group, igniting some heated words and some diss tracks made by Buck. In 2014, the pair were seen performing at iHeartRadio Music festival, seemingly having squashed any disagreements, however, in the following years, it appears the two remained at odds with one another.

Interestingly enough, this is not the first line written by G Herbo that has mentioned both Young Buck and 50 Cent. For his verse on the Skilla Baby song “Mike Jack,” released in April 2024, Herbo rapped:

Like he discovered Young Buck, done fucked up many men

This is a reference to 50 signing Young Buck, as well as the former’s hit song, “Many Men (Wish Death)” from May 2003.
